links.outcome: Calibration of LLM confidence estimates for deprescribing recommendations
links.effect: Confidence poorly calibrated; severely left-skewed with minimum confidence 58.5% (eligibility) and 54.5% (deprescribing); selective prediction only marginally improved performance.
links.quote: However, despite some minor improvements, we find that the LLM is poorly calibrated, as shown in Figure 6 B.

links.outcome: LLM making deprescribing recommendations, including potentially harmful ones, on clinical cases
links.effect: Deprescribing step PPV 0.47; LLM recommended deprescribing far more often (11.6%) than students (1.91%); harmful cases observed, e.g., suggesting deprescribing anticoagulation after recent thromboembolism.
links.quote: Cases with the potential for human harm were observed, such as suggesting deprescribing anticoagulation in a patient with recent thromboembolism.

links.outcome: Selective prediction (abstention/deferral to humans) effect on LLM F1 performance
links.effect: Consistency-based deferral raised F1 to 0.85-0.88 (step 1) and 0.62-0.73 (step 2); verbalized confidence gave narrower ranges (0.58-0.69 step 2); gains marginal due to poor calibration.
links.quote: Selective prediction marginally improved the LLM’s filtering accuracy by enabling it to defer uncertain cases to human reviewers.

links.outcome: LLM application of deprescribing criteria to patient cases, error types
links.effect: Errors due to complex inclusion/exclusion criteria (54.5%) and ambiguous clinical contexts such as missing information (39.3%); step 2 PPV 0.47, F1 0.58.
links.quote: Adjudication revealed that while the model excelled at identifying when there was a deprescribing criterion related to one of the patient's medications, it often struggled with determining whether that criterion applied to the specific case due to complex inclusion and exclusion criteria (54.5% of errors) and ambiguous clinical contexts (eg, missing information; 39.3% of errors).

links.outcome: LLM versus medical students on criteria filtering and deprescribing recommendation, adjudicated
links.effect: LLM better at criteria filtering (80.1% vs 59.5% correct, P=.02) but worse, not significantly, at applying criteria (P=.178).
links.quote: However, in applying relevant criteria, GPT-4o performed worse than the medical students, though the difference was not statistically significant (McNemar test: χ 2 1 =1.818; P =.178).

links.outcome: Interrater reliability of junior annotators motivating senior adjudication as gold standard
links.effect: Medical student IRR was low (Cohen k step 1=0.68, step 2=0.33), so physician adjudication was used; senior IRR 0.795 and 0.745.
links.quote: Adjudication was chosen as the gold standard for resolving discrepancies because preliminary research showed low IRR among medical students for both steps of the process (Cohen k : step 1=0.68, step 2=0.33) across 75 medications.

links.outcome: Potential alert burden from inaccurate LLM deprescribing recommendations
links.effect: LLM over-recommended deprescribing (11.6% vs 1.91% for students); authors note inaccuracies could increase alert fatigue and interpretation time.
links.quote: If implemented in clinical decision support, these inaccuracies might contribute to increased alert fatigue and extend the time required to interpret LLM-generated recommendations, potentially offsetting the intended efficiency gains in identifying deprescribing opportunities.

Consistency-based (self-sampling) confidence elicitation for selective prediction

links.outcome: case-specific deprescribing recommendations
links.effect: Criteria identification PPV 0.83, NPV 0.93; recommendations PPV 0.47, NPV 0.93.
links.quote: The LLM was significantly more effective in identifying deprescribing criteria (positive predictive value: 0.83; negative predictive value: 0.93; McNemar test for paired proportions: χ<sup>2</sup><sub>1</sub>=5.985; P=.02) relative to medical students, but showed limitations in making specific deprescribing recommendations (positive predictive value=0.47; negative predictive value=0.93).

links.outcome: confidence-based deferral performance
links.effect: Verbalized F1 step 2: 0.58–0.69; consistency-based F1 step 2: 0.62–0.73; improvement was marginal.
links.quote: Selective prediction only marginally improved LLM performance due to poorly calibrated confidence estimates.

links.outcome: confidence calibration
links.effect: Minimum confidence was 58.5% for eligibility filtering and 54.5% for deprescribing recommendations.
links.quote: Despite consistency-based weighting, the confidence distribution is severely left-skewed with the minimum confidence being 58.5% in eligibility filtering and 54.5% in deprescribing recommendations.

links.outcome: deprescribing recommendation accuracy
links.effect: Recommendation task F1-score 0.58, precision=0.47, recall=0.76.
links.quote: In this second step, which involved applying relevant criteria to make a recommendation, the LLM performed less effectively, with an F 1 -score of 0.58 (precision=0.47, recall=0.76).

links.outcome: errors from missing or ambiguous data
links.effect: Complex inclusion/exclusion caused 54.5% of errors; ambiguous contexts including missing information caused 39.3%.
links.quote: Adjudication revealed that while the model excelled at identifying when there was a deprescribing criterion related to one of the patient's medications, it often struggled with determining whether that criterion applied to the specific case due to complex inclusion and exclusion criteria (54.5% of errors) and ambiguous clinical contexts (eg, missing information; 39.3% of errors).

links.outcome: deprescribing accuracy across deferral fractions using selective prediction
links.effect: Consistency-based selective prediction marginally increased F1-scores from 0.85 to 0.88 for criteria filtering and from 0.62 to 0.73 for deprescribing recommendations as deferral increased, limited by poor confidence calibration.
links.quote: Selective prediction only marginally improved LLM performance due to poorly calibrated confidence estimates.

links.outcome: LLM confidence calibration and overconfidence
links.effect: GPT-4o showed poor confidence calibration with a minimum confidence of 54% even when deprescribing recommendations were incorrect, indicating overconfidence.
links.quote: Specifically, the LLM displayed a minimum confidence level of 54%, even in cases where its recommendations were incorrect.
